before.exam_tip_html: When answering an AO2 language question, do not try to cover every technique in the extract. Pick 3–4 well-chosen examples and analyse each one in depth. The examiner rewards quality of analysis over quantity of points. A response that deeply analyses three word choices will outscore one that names eight techniques without explaining their effects.

If you can only make one point about sentence structure, make it about a shift — a change from long to short sentences, or from declarative to interrogative. Examiners reward students who can explain why the writer changes their sentence patterns at a specific moment in the extract.

When answering a question about structure on Paper 2, avoid simply listing structural features. The examiner rewards analysis of effect. Use the formula: identify the structural choice → explain why the writer made it → analyse its effect on the reader. For example: “The writer opens with a one-sentence paragraph — ‘Nobody listened.’ — to create a stark, isolated statement that immediately establishes the sense of frustration that drives the rest of the article.”

In the comparison question, aim for at least three well-developed paragraphs. Each paragraph should: (1) make a comparative point about both writers, (2) include evidence from both texts, (3) analyse the methods used, and (4) connect those methods to the writers’ ideas and perspectives. Do not write about ideas and methods in separate sections — integrate them. The examiner rewards responses that show how a writer’s method serves their message.

Do not try to name every technique in the text. Select the three or four most significant techniques and analyse them in depth. The examiner rewards quality of analysis over quantity of technique identification. For every term you use, include a specific example from the text and a detailed explanation of its effect on the reader. One well-analysed rhetorical question is worth more than five techniques named without explanation.
